Investing in the public benefit \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Skip to footer
Try Claude
Announcements
Investing in the public benefit
Oct 18, 2026
Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund,
a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed
$200 million
to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

items.title: An update on independent evaluators
items.content:
Anthropic update on independent evaluators \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Skip to footer
Try Claude
Announcements
An update on independent evaluators
Oct 15, 2026
Last month, we committed to
stronger independent, third-party assessment
of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from
METR
, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.
METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on
several reviews of our Risk Reports
. We’re also working with
SecureBio
and
Accenture
as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including
Hugging Face
.
Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.
Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.
To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:
Expertise
in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as
alignment faking
.
Independence
: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
Enough
access
to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
Freedom to publish
observations and assessments
of a model or a process.
Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.
For the AI industry, this is a step toward
robust safety oversight
. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.
What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.
1
METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories such as reproducing confidential IP. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)
2
Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.
Our other evaluator partnerships
We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.
We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.
In the first tier,
evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.
In the second tier,
evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.
The third tier
is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.
SecureBio
is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our
August Risk Report
, after completing and
publishing a pilot review
of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.
3
With Accenture
and Faculty, we're working
toward an ambitious partnership
that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.
We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.
Footnotes
Because these evaluators (like bank examiners) may also work with other companies, we exercise caution around the possibility of inadvertent leaks. Information about architectures presents a high risk of inadvertent leaks, and its relevance to risk assessment is typically low. When it is highly relevant, we will generally seek to share it, though this will require explicit internal approvals.
Updated on October 16 to clarify METR's current project terms with Anthropic.
Updated on October 15 to clarify SecureBio's current project terms with Anthropic.

items.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
items.content:
Preparing for the 2026 US midterms \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Skip to footer
Try Claude
Policy
Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
Oct 14, 2026
Earlier this year, we shared an
update on our election safeguards
, which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.
Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
How people use Claude for elections and politics
Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.
1
Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to
increase
.
This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our
election integrity policies
were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.
2
How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for.
Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using
a privacy-preserving method
. Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies.
What people ask Claude for in political conversations.
Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through
Anthropic Insights
.
Connecting people to trusted sources
Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from
Democracy Works
.
Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.
Official voting information presented by Democracy Works.
Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.
Measuring and preventing political bias
When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our
political evenhandedness evaluation
.
Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.
As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies.
The Future of Free Speech
, an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the
Foundation for American Innovation
compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The
Collective Intelligence Project
surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.
These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.
We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.
How we define misuse
Our
Usage Policy
prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we
announced
last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.
We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently
published a guide
to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.
Testing and strengthening our defenses
We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the
Institute for Strategic Dialogue
(ISD) and the
McCain Institute
, both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.
Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.
Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share
examples
of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.
What we've found
Our recent
threat intelligence report
reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.
Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.
Looking ahead
More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.
Footnotes
We took a random sample of 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026 and analyzed them in a privacy-preserving way.
This figure was generated from a separate analysis of 250,000 Claude.ai conversations, which were reviewed against our election integrity policy.

NVIDIA CUDA Tile
(cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model that abstracts thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives to automatically target Tensor Cores and other advanced GPU hardware features.
Machine learning engineers at
Jane Street
implemented the Mamba-2 state-space model in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize three custom kernels for the forward pass: chunk_cumsum, fwd_pass_state, and compute_out.
The chunk_cumsum kernel computes per-token, per-head cumulative sums of the decay term in log-space using ct.cumsum, storing results for reuse by the subsequent kernels.
The fwd_pass_state kernel uses ct.mma to execute Tensor Core matrix-multiply operations that advance the hidden state across sequence chunks, applying the jump formula with exponential decay and pre-multiplied operands.
The compute_out kernel fuses the carried-state term, the decayed and causally masked interaction matrix, and the skip connection into a single tiled kernel that keeps intermediate matrices in registers and casts to TF32 for Tensor Core execution.
Performance optimizations include latency hints for DRAM traffic modeling, operand swapping to route fused operands to Tensor Memory, transposed memory layouts for TMA-friendly access, and an autotuner that searches block size and occupancy parameters for each input shape.

NVIDIA CUDA Tile
(cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores.
As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at
Jane Street
implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them.
Overview and prerequisites
To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the
cuTile Python Quickstart
guide. Import the package as
cuda.tile
and expose it as
ct
throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post.
Sequence modeling computational trade-off
Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length.
Mamba-2 architecture
The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores.
The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is:
\(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\)

t

c

⊤

D

y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t
Where:
\(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\)
\(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\)
\(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity)
\(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters
Intuitively:
\(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\)
\(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention
\(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention
\(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention
The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size
S,H
(\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply:
\(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\)
This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores.
An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just:
\(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\)
If building a matrix \(B\) of shape (
T, S
) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape (
T, H
) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\):
Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events
With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given
only
\(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula.
Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute:
\(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\)
Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this:
Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states
Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention).
When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection):
\(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
With \(M\) the traditional causal mask.
Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation
Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like:
\(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\)
Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation:
\(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\)
Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following:
\(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability.
Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe
This will translate into three kernels:
chunk_cumsum
: Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk.
fwd_pass_state
: Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above.
compute_out
: Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step.
Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums
The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk.
The inputs to this kernel are a per-head scalar decay
a
and a per-token timestep
dt
. The effective decay at token
t
for head
h
is
a[h] * dt[t, h]
, and the kernel accumulates that product along the chunk dimension. These cumulative sums are all in log-space and the exponential of them is always taken (or some linear combination of them). Since it’s much cheaper to compute
exp2
instead of
exp
, the result is scaled by
log2(e)
.
This kernel introduces the cuTile primitives that all three kernels use:
ct.bid
,
ct.load
/
ct.store
, and
ct.cumsum
.
The full kernel is short:
@ct.kernel
def chunk_cumsum_kernel(
a: torch.Tensor,        # [num_heads]
dt: torch.Tensor,       # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads]
output: torch.Tensor,   # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads]
chunk_size: ct.Constant[int],
BLOCK_H: ct.Constant[int],
) -> None:
chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2)
dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx),
shape=(1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H),
padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32)
a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(head_tile_idx,),
shape=(BLOCK_H,),
padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32)
d_tile = ct.cumsum(a_tile * dt_tile, axis=1) * LOG2E
ct.store(output, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), tile=d_tile.astype(output.dtype))
The kernel is launched with a grid of
(num_chunks, num_head_tiles, batch_size)
, the first line determines where you are in the grid using
ct.bid
. The broadcast product of
a_tile
(shape
[BLOCK_H]
) and
dt_tile
(shape
[1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H]
) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile.
ct.cumsum(..., axis=1)
then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by
fwd_pass_state
and
compute_out
.
Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state

computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that
compute_ou

(batch, head, head_tile, state_tile)
slice of the hidden state, as shown below. Within that slice,
hid_tile

[BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE]
and will contain a tile of the initial hidden state for each chunk.

combines the GB10 system-on-a-chip with up to 128GB of unified memory to let developers run local coding agents, test, and deploy on a single PC.
The platform delivers 4.6x faster coding-agent performance, 2.7x faster fine-tuning, and 1.8x faster code compilation compared with Intel Panther Lake 12Xe.
NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to expand the Windows on Arm software stack, adding the first PyTorch-CUDA build, Python 3.15 native by default, over 2,000 Conda packages, and Arm-compatible versions for more than 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74B-parameter mixture-of-experts model quantized to 2 bits, is purpose-built for local agents on RTX Spark and runs on llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, and LM Studio.
Decision models now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth enable agents to choose actions up to 200x faster than traditional reasoning loops.
NVIDIA AI for Media SDKs with video super resolution, frame generation, and TrueHDR are available on RTX Spark via PyPI and NGC.
Next Steps
Explore
RTX Spark systems
to find available purchasing options.
Follow the
AI Development playbook
to configure Windows, set up your agent, and connect NVIDIA Skills.
Learn about
developing Local AI apps
for NVIDIA GPUs.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
AI agents are changing how software gets built. Developers have gone from writing every line of code by hand to directing agents that write most of the code. As a result, the current workflow is split across a laptop, a cloud model API, and a cloud VM.
NVIDIA RTX Spark
is built for AI development. Thanks to the NVIDIA GB10 system-on-a-chip and large unified memory, developers can run local coding agents, access AI frameworks, and code, test, and deploy on a single PC.
One machine to code, test, and deploy
RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops enable developers to complete all of their workflow on a single machine.
Developers can choose to work in Windows, including the new Windows Developer Config, developed with Microsoft, which installs the top development frameworks, mutes notifications, enhances the terminal, and can move their task bar to the side. Or they can work in Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they get access to the same environment and dependencies they will use when deploying to the cloud.
This enables developers to complete all their work in their target OS without code migrations. And since RTX Spark has an NVIDIA GPU, developers can test and deploy to the largest local AI installed base: 150 million RTX PCs, as well as virtually all the clouds in the world that run on NVIDIA GPUs.
With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI compute, developers can run coding models locally, including Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, reducing cloud coding agent token consumption.
The performance you need for AI development
Development has gone from being a CPU-bound workload, where performance was determined mostly by the CPU, to a GPU-bound workload. AI developers today need to run inference to run their coding agents and test their apps; for fine-tuning and training models; and yes, still a bit of compilation.
Thanks to the NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU in RTX Spark, these laptops and desktops come equipped with all the compute required for inference, fine-tuning and compilation. Compared with Intel’s Panther Lake 12Xe, RTX Spark delivers 4.6x performance on coding agents, 2.7x performance on fine-tuning, and 1.8x performance on code compilation.
Figure 1. NVIDIA developer-workload comparison, with Intel Core Ultra X9 388H normalized to 1.0. Tests: AA-AgentPerf-local with Qwen3.8-27B; Unsloth LoRA with Llama-3.1-8B; and Linux kernel compilation using Phoronix Test Suite
A familiar software stack, expanded for Windows
NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to advance the Windows on Arm developer landscape. Together with RTX Spark, the community is releasing multiple new tools, including the first PyTorch-CUDA build, the first Python release that is native by default with Python 3.15, over 2,000 ready-to-use Conda packages, and Arm-compatible versions for more than 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages.
A key advantage of developing on NVIDIA hardware is access to the largest ecosystem of developer tools, from coding agents, to AI models, to frameworks.
Because NVIDIA GPUs are the most widely used platform for AI development, new tools and frameworks typically work on NVIDIA from day one, while support for other hardware follows weeks later. There’s also access to NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including tools such as FlashInfer for LLM acceleration and NVIDIA NeMo libraries tools for AI model development.
NVIDIA also provides a repository of
NVIDIA Skills
that teach agents how to use CUDA-X libraries, enabling developers to build GPU-accelerated applications without requiring deep familiarity with CUDA.
Figure 2. RTX Spark’s ecosystem of agents, models, frameworks, and CUDA-X libraries
Local coding agents come to RTX Spark
RTX Spark devices are ideal for local coding agents. NVIDIA has collaborated closely with the top agents, including GitHub Copilot, Pi, Hermes, and OpenClaw, to improve them and make them easier to use.
The improvements include:
Seamless deployment of local models with optimized recipes
Enhanced security with NVIDIA OpenShell and/or Microsoft Execution Containers, delivering OS-level sandboxing
Hybrid prompt routers between local and cloud models, so that prompts get sent to local models if they are good enough, or escalated to cloud if needed, reducing token consumption
Microsoft GitHub CoPilot now enables seamless local AI through Windows ML, which is now supported with llama.cpp as a backend. The prompt router HydraFusion has been upgraded to also support local models. And the new MAI 1.1 Coding Flash model can run locally on RTX Spark.
Pi
, an open-source coding agent with a lightweight terminal interface and support for local and cloud models, is also optimized for RTX Spark. Its extensions, skills, and prompt templates give developers control over how the agent fits into their workflow, from model selection to the tools it can use.
JetBrains has launched native support for
Junie Local on RTX Spark
. The coding agent reads code, edits files, and runs tests, with the model and code staying on the machine. Junie Local sizes its context window to the memory available to the GPU, so RTX Spark unified memory lets it keep more code, tool output, and conversation history in context.
New Nemotron models offer more options for local agents
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark.
This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.
Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw.
Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source, including training data, weights and recipes, so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.
Decision models now supported in top frameworks
Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests, to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in
llama.cpp
and
Unsloth
on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs.
AI for media SDKs
The
NVIDIA AI for Media SDKs
are now available for RTX Spark, including Python wheel with support for video super resolution, frame generation, and TrueHDR. The wheel is available on PyPI, with C++ SDKs also available on NGC for RTX Spark and Windows on Arm.
Bring your Windows applications to RTX Spark
To bring an existing application to RTX Spark, first assess dependencies for Windows on Arm. Choose a native Arm64 build or use Arm64EC to migrate components incrementally. Test installation, functionality, performance, and the NVIDIA and CUDA paths your app uses.
NVIDIA’s app-porting resources
explain the migration options and tools, including how to start preparation on an existing Windows on Arm development system.
Find your RTX Spark and start building
RTX Spark is available now in laptops, and coming in November to small form factor desktops that are ideal for always on, 24×7 running agents.
Explore RTX Spark systems
to find your favorite and see available purchasing options.
Once you get your own, get started with the
AI Development playbook
to configure Windows, set up your agent, and connect NVIDIA Skills. And learn about how you can get started

for NVIDIA GPUs.

This procedure covers upgrading from Apigee hybrid
version 1.15.x to Apigee hybrid version 1.16.11 and
from previous releases of hybrid 1.16.x to version
1.16.11.
Use the same procedures for minor version upgrades (for example version 1.15
to 1.16) and for patch release upgrades (for example
1.16.0 to 1.16.11).
If you are upgrading from Apigee hybrid version 1.14 or older, you must first upgrade to
hybrid version 1.15 before upgrading to version 1.16.11.
See the instructions for
Upgrading
Apigee hybrid to version 1.15
.
Changes from Apigee hybrid v1.15
Please note the following changes:
Seccomp profiles
:
Starting in
version 1.16
,
Apigee hybrid now offers the capability to apply Seccomp Profiles to your runtime components,
significantly enhancing the security posture of your deployment. This feature allows Apigee
administrators and security teams to restrict the system calls a containerized process can make
to the host's kernel. By limiting a container to only the necessary syscalls, you can:
Enhance Security: Mitigate the risk of container breakouts and privilege escalation.
Enforce Least Privilege: Ensure components only have access to the exact system calls
required for their operation.
Meet Compliance: Provide a critical control for meeting stringent security compliance
requirements.
For more information, see
Configure Seccomp profiles for
pod security
.
UDCA in Apigee hybrid removal
:
In Apigee hybrid
version 1.16
,
the Unified Data Collection Agent (UDCA) component has been removed. The responsibilities of
sending analytics, trace, and deployment status data to the Apigee control plane are now handled
using a
Google Cloud Pub/Sub
based data pipeline. Using the Pub/Sub
based data pipeline has been the default data collection mechanism since Apigee hybrid
version 1.14.0
.
apigee-guardrails
service account
:
In v1.16.0, Apigee Hybrid introduces an
apigee-guardrails
Google IAM service account. This is used by the
apigee-operator
chart during installation to check that all needed APIs are enabled in your project.
See:
Diagnosing issues with guardrails
About service accounts:
apigee-guardrails
create-service-account
Installation Part 2: Step 4: Create service accounts
Installation Part 2: Step 5: Set up service account authentication
Support for cert-manager release 1.18 and 1.19
:
Apigee hybrid v1.16 supports cert-manager
release 1.18
and
release 1.19
. In cert-manager release 1.18, there is a change to the default value of
Certificate.Spec.PrivateKey.rotationPolicy
that can impact traffic. If you are upgrading from a previous version of Apigee hybrid, and you are uprading to cert-manager release 1.18 or above, follow the
Upgrade cert-manager
prodedure in this guide.
Note:
This does not affect fresh installations of Apigee hybrid v1.6.
For additional information about features in Hybrid version 1.16, see the
Apigee hybrid
v1.16.11 release notes
.
Prerequisites
Before upgrading to hybrid version 1.16, make sure your
installation meets the following requirements:
If your hybrid installation is running a version older than v1.15, you
must upgrade to version 1.15 before upgrading to v1.16.
See
Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version 1.15
.
Helm version v3.14.2+.
kubectl
: A supported version of
kubectl
appropriate for your Kubernetes platform version. See
Supported platforms and versions:
kubectl
.
cert-manager: A supported version of cert-manager. See
Supported platforms and versions: cert-manager
. If needed, you will upgrade cert-manager in the
Prepare to upgrade to version 1.16
section below.
Before you upgrade to 1.16.11 - limitations and important notes
Apigee hybrid 1.16.11 introduces a new enhanced per-environment
proxy limit that lets you deploy more proxies and shared flows in a single
environment.  See
Limits: API Proxies
to understand the limits on the number of proxies and shared flows you may deploy per
environment.  This feature is available only on newly created hybrid organizations,
and cannot be applied to upgraded orgs. To use this feature, perform a fresh
installation of hybrid 1.16.11, and create a new organization.
This feature is available exclusively as part of the
2024 subscription plan
,
and is subject to the entitlements granted under that subscription. See
Enhanced per-environment proxy limits
to learn more about this feature.
Upgrading to Apigee hybrid version 1.16 may require
downtime.
When upgrading the Apigee controller to version 1.16.11, all Apigee
deployments undergo a rolling restart. To minimize downtime in production hybrid environments
during a rolling restart, make sure you are running at least two clusters (in the same or
different region/data center). Divert all production traffic to a single cluster and take the
cluster you are about to upgrade offline, and then proceed with the upgrade process. Repeat
the process for each cluster.
Apigee recommends that once you begin the upgrade, you should upgrade all clusters as soon as possible to reduce the chances
of production impact. There is no time limit on when all remaining clusters must be upgraded
after the first one is upgraded. However, until all remaining clusters are upgraded Cassandra
backup and restore cannot work with mixed versions. For example, a backup from Hybrid
1.15 cannot be used to restore a Hybrid 1.16
instance.
Management plane changes do not need to be fully suspended during an upgrade.
Any required temporary suspensions to management plane changes are noted in the upgrade
instructions below.
Upgrading to version 1.16.11 overview
The procedures for upgrading Apigee hybrid are organized in the following sections:
Prepare to upgrade
.
Install hybrid runtime version 1.16.11
.
Prepare to upgrade to version 1.16
Back up your hybrid installation
These instructions use the environment variable
APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
for the directory
in your file system where you have installed the Helm charts. If needed, change directory
into this directory and define the variable with the following command:
Linux
export APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=$PWD
echo
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
Mac OS
export APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=$PWD
echo
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
Windows
set APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=%CD%
echo %APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME%
Make a backup copy of your version 1.15
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME/
directory. You can use any backup process. For example,
you can create a
tar
file of your entire directory with:
tar -czvf
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
/../apigee-helm-charts-v1.15-backup.tar.gz
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME

Conversational analytics, powered by
Gemini for Google Cloud
, lets you investigate your data by asking questions about it in conversational language through an intuitive chat interface. Conversational analytics provides multiple ways to "converse" with your data. When using Conversational Analytics with Explore data, you can ask questions about a single Explore in a conversation or create an Explore data agent to chat with as many as five Explores at once. You can also use Explore data agents that other users have created and shared with you.
Note:
This page refers to Explore data agents — data agents that query Explores. For information about data agents that query user-defined and LookML dashboards, see the
Query a user-defined dashboard with a dashboard agent
and
Create and manage data agents for LookML dashboards
documentation pages, respectively.
This page discusses how to use Conversational Analytics to engage with Explore data. It covers the following topics:
Starting a conversation with a single Explore
Start a conversation with an existing data agent that queries Explores
Asking questions about your data
Managing queries within a conversation
Understanding query results and calculations
Managing conversations
Learn
how and when Gemini
for Google Cloud uses your data
.
As an early-stage technology, Gemini for Google Cloud
products can generate output that seems plausible but is factually incorrect. We recommend that you
validate all output from Gemini for Google Cloud products before you use it.
For more information, see
Gemini for Google Cloud and responsible AI
.
Before you begin
Before you can use Conversational Analytics to engage with your Explore data, make sure that the
setup and requirements for your Looker instance
have been satisfied and that you have been granted the
appropriate permissions
to perform the tasks that are described on this page.
Start a conversation with a single Explore
To start a conversation — a discrete set of questions and answers about your data in regular, natural language in a chat interface — with a single Explore, follow these steps:
Navigate to the Conversational Analytics interface.
From the
main navigation menu
: Select
Conversations
. Select the

items.title: Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK The open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) and gemini-3.8-live enable developers to build responsive voice
items.content:
Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK
- Google Developers Blog
Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK
OCT. 19, 2026
Stephen Allen
Solutions Architect
AI Apps and Platforms
Kaz Sato
Staff Developer Advocate
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Building a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent with ADK and Gemini 3.8 Live
A guide to
streaming tools
, non-blocking function calls, and response scheduling in the
Agent Development Kit (ADK) Gemini Live API Toolkit
.
In text chat, a 13-second database query or RAG pipeline shows a loading spinner. In a live voice conversation, 13 seconds of blocking tool execution produces 13 seconds of dead air, causing users to assume the call dropped and hang up.
You cannot always make backend queries sub-second, so the fix must be architectural: keep the agent conversational while slow tools run in the background. Rather than forcing you to wire up custom client-side WebSocket event loops to manage asynchronous tool state, the open-source ADK and gemini-3.8-live let you implement non-blocking voice tools natively in Python. In our benchmark sales-report workflow on gemini-3.8-live, switching from a blocking tool to a streaming tool cut the time to the agent's first words from 14.4 seconds to 1.2 seconds.
This guide covers how to use streaming tools, non-blocking FunctionTool definitions, and response_scheduling to build responsive, natural voice agents.
Watch the 1-minute ADK Live AI Concierge demo video to hear scheduled responses in action:
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
ADK Live AI Concierge demo video explains how scheduled responses work
What Non-Blocking Tools Enable
Implementing non-blocking tool calls in ADK provides several immediate user experience benefits:
Zero Dead Air:
Instead of freezing mid-conversation, the agent can acknowledge requests immediately ("Looking into those numbers now...") and keep the dialogue alive.
Audible Progress Updates:
For multi-stage workflows (such as connecting, querying, and reconciling), the agent can narrate interim milestones so the wait sounds like active progress.
Multitasking and Parallel Dialogue:
Users can ask follow-up or unrelated questions while a long-running query executes in the background, and receive timely answers without stalling the session.
Granular Delivery Control:
You determine when and how the final result enters the conversation: waiting for a natural speaking pause, interrupting immediately for critical alerts, or silently updating conversation context.
The Baseline: Why Standard Tools Block Conversation
In standard agent development, a tool is defined as an async def function that completes its work and returns a single value:
from typing import Any
async def query_sales_database(region: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
"""Runs the quarterly sales report query for a region.
Args:
region: Sales region to report on, e.g. "EMEA" or "APAC".
Returns:
A dict containing report metrics upon completion.
"""
report = await run_expensive_query(region)       # e.g., 13 seconds of work
return {"status": "success", "report": report}   # Single return at the end
Plain text
Copied
When passed directly to an
Agent
in ADK, this function creates a blocking tool call. During a Gemini Live API bidirectional voice session (
run_live
), the execution loop awaits the tool's return before generating further model turns.
If
query_sales_database
takes 13 seconds, the agent produces 13 seconds of complete silence. Prompting instructions such as "tell the user you are working on it" cannot resolve this, because the model's turn is blocked waiting for the function response payload.
To keep the conversation fluid, you can choose between two main non-blocking patterns depending on the desired user experience.
Pattern 1: Streaming Tools (When Progress Has a Story)
When an operation consists of meaningful stages (such as connecting to a database, aggregating records, and formatting results), a
streaming tool
lets the agent narrate progress as it happens.
In ADK, turning a standard tool into a streaming tool requires changing only
return
to
yield
. By defining the function as an
AsyncGenerator
, ADK automatically marks the tool declaration as
NON_BLOCKING
and returns an immediate status acknowledgement to the model.
import asyncio
from typing import AsyncGenerator
from google.adk.agents import Agent
async def query_sales_database(region: str) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]:
"""Runs the quarterly sales report. Call this ONCE; it pushes updates automatically.
Args:
region: Sales region to report on, e.g. "EMEA" or "APAC".
Yields:
Progress updates while the query runs, followed by the final summary.
"""
stages = [
("Connecting to the sales warehouse...", 1.5),
("Scanning order records...", 3.5),
("Aggregating revenue by product line...", 3.5),
("Formatting the report...", 1.5),
]
for message, delay in stages:
yield f"PROGRESS: {message}"
await asyncio.sleep(delay)
yield f"DONE: {region} Q2 revenue reached $4.81M, up 12.4% year over year."
agent = Agent(
name="sales_analyst",
model="gemini-3.8-live",
tools=[query_sales_database],
instruction=(
"You are a helpful sales assistant. When the user asks about sales data, "
"call query_sales_database once. Acknowledge the request immediately, "
"briefly paraphrase each progress update, and present the final figures "
"when completed. Keep answers conversational and concise."
),
)
Plain text
Copied
How It Works in Practice
Immediate Acknowledgment:
When the model triggers
query_sales_database
, ADK immediately dispatches an asynchronous status event to the model. The agent speaks right away ("Looking into the EMEA figures for you now...").
Partial Updates:
Each
yield
sends a partial function response upstream. The model paraphrases each update as it arrives ("Connecting to the warehouse...", "Aggregating product line data..."), though narration can trail the tool by several seconds.
Seamless Multi-Threading:
If the user asks an unrelated question while the query is running, the agent can answer it without canceling or interrupting the background task.
Production Considerations for Streaming Tools
Single-Flight Tool Calls:
Because streaming tools push updates across multiple turns, models may occasionally attempt to call the tool again if prompted repeatedly. Keep a clear "Call this ONCE" directive in your docstring, and consider implementing an in-memory latch or idempotency key in your tool implementation for production safety.
User Cancellation with `stop_streaming`:
ADK provides a built-in escape hatch for long-running streaming tools. By including a function named
stop_streaming(function_name: str)
in the agent's tools list, ADK intercepts the call and cancels the generator's underlying
asyncio.Task
, raising
asyncio.CancelledError
within your function so you can cleanly close database connections or file handles.
User Barge-In Does Not Cancel Tools:
When the user talks over the agent, the Live API stops the model's output and ADK emits an event with
interrupted=True
so your client can stop audio playback. Running streaming or background tools are not cancelled, and their results are still delivered. To stop a tool, the model must call
stop_streaming
.
Pattern 2: Background Execution (When Waiting Is Just Waiting)
Continuous progress commentary is not always appropriate. If a user asks for a report and immediately pivots to another topic, an agent that continually interrupts with status updates can feel intrusive.
When the wait has no story to narrate, run the task quietly in the background.
Approach A: The Single-Yield Generator (Fastest Setup)
An effective way to get an immediate verbal acknowledgment without ongoing progress chatter is an async generator that yields only once, upon completion:
async def query_sales_database(region: str) -> AsyncGenerator[dict, None]:
"""Runs the quarterly sales report. Call this ONCE; results arrive when ready."""
report = await run_expensive_query(region)   # Background execution (~13s)
yield report                                 # Single yield upon completion
Plain text
Copied
Because this is an async generator, ADK issues an immediate pending response. The agent promptly acknowledges the request ("I'm pulling that report together for you now"), remains silent during computation, and presents the figures once ready or when the user finishes speaking.
Approach B: `FunctionTool` with `response_scheduling`
If you prefer to keep standard coroutines (
async def ... -> dict
), wrap the function in a
FunctionTool
and configure
response_scheduling
:
from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool
from google.genai import types
sales_tool = FunctionTool(query_sales_database)
sales_tool.response_scheduling = types.FunctionResponseScheduling.WHEN_IDLE
(Note: In ADK 2.10+, you can also set `sales_tool.behavior = types.Behavior.NON_BLOCKING` to run a tool in the background without modifying scheduling mode.)
Plain text
Copied
Understanding the Trade-Off:
When using
response_scheduling
with a return-once coroutine, the model receives no payload until the entire function completes. As a result, the model typically does not utter an initial verbal acknowledgment unless the user continues speaking. This pattern is ideal when the user immediately continues with other questions and you want the result woven into the dialogue at the next natural pause.
Controlling Result Delivery with `response_scheduling`
The
response_scheduling
attribute controls
when
the model reacts to an incoming tool response.
WHEN_IDLE
never cuts into a turn in progress: if the model is still speaking or the user is still talking, the result waits until that turn ends, and the model responds at the next natural pause. ADK supports three scheduling behaviors:
In benchmark sessions with
gemini-3.8
-live:
Under
WHEN_IDLE
, an incoming sales report waited politely while the model finished answering a separate 20-second question, then delivered the figures seamlessly.
Under
INTERRUPT
, the incoming result cut off current speech mid-sentence; the model then finished its answer and appended the figures.
Under
SILENT
, the result was added to the conversation history, available for subsequent turns without prompting an unrequested announcement.
Combining Streaming and Scheduling
Execution shape (streaming vs. single-return) and delivery timing (
response_scheduling
) are independent and can be composed. Setting
response_scheduling
on a streaming tool stamps every partial update with that behavior.
Furthermore, in ADK 2.8 and newer, streaming tools can dynamically specify scheduling per update by yielding
types.FunctionResponse
:
# Acknowledge and keep intermediate progress quiet:
yield types.FunctionResponse(
response={"stage": "aggregating"},
scheduling=types.FunctionResponseScheduling.SILENT,
)
# Deliver the final result when the speaker finishes:
yield types.FunctionResponse(
response={"report": final_data},
scheduling=types.FunctionResponseScheduling.WHEN_IDLE,
)
Plain text
Copied
Architecture Summary: Choosing the Right Tool Pattern
The rule of thumb:
If the wait has a story, stream it. If the wait is just a wait, run it in the background and let the result land when idle.
Conclusion
Non-blocking tools do not reduce backend execution time: a 13-second query still takes 13 seconds. What changes is the conversational presence of your agent.
A web application that takes ten seconds to load is perceived as slow; a conversational voice agent that goes silent for ten seconds is perceived as broken. By pairing ADK's streaming tools and flexible response scheduling with the real-time capabilities of
gemini-3.8-live
, you can build voice assistants that remain attentive, natural, and present throughout complex operations.
Try it yourself:
the
interactive demo
runs the same 13-second query through every tool pattern and response_scheduling mode on gemini-3.8-live, so you can hear the difference.
Requirements & Next Steps
Framework:
google-adk >= 2.10.0

items.title: Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API Meet the LiteRT Tensor API: giving developers native C++ control over the model graph to unify end-to-end ML computations on
items.content:
Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API
- Google Developers Blog
Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API
OCT. 19, 2026
Ping Yu
Staff Software Engineer
Quentin Khan
Sr. Software Engineer
Chintan Parikh
Sr. Product Manager
Lu Wang
Sr. Staff Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Shipping on-device AI means meeting tight latency and memory budgets on every device you target. The most common path for deploying models in production is converting a trained model, for example converting a PyTorch model with
LiteRT Torch
, and running it with the
LiteRT runtime
. This offers the quickest and most reliable route to production, and it's the path we recommend for most projects. Sometimes, though, developers want full control over how a network is represented and optimized to support new architectures or to try a new lowering logic without waiting for upstream framework updates.
For ultimate control, developers write computations manually in native C++ or shader languages.
Apple's MLX
made this code-first approach popular on Apple silicon, and
llama.cpp
showed how far tailored C++ implementations can take LLM inference. However, the level of control comes at a significant cost: implementations are tightly coupled to specific backends (such as Metal, OpenCL, or Vulkan) and must be rewritten for each new hardware target. Furthermore, managing zero-copy buffer interoperability and synchronization across CPU, GPU, and NPU, while gluing together pre-processing, inference, and post-processing, demands substantial manual engineering effort.
To solve the above challenges, we are excited to announce the release of the novel
LiteRT Tensor API
, a lightweight authoring layer in the LiteRT stack, designed to improve handcrafting models. It combines the flexibility of native authoring with cross-platform portability. You build the computation graph op by op in C++, choosing exactly which ops run and how they connect. The same graph can run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU (powered by open-source
ML Drift
) and NPU, or without model file or runtime directly on CPU through XNNPACK, so you don't rewrite it for each new hardware target. Model inference and pre/post-processing can be assembled with the same API and chained through shared accelerator buffers, so that data never round-trips through the CPU. Start with the conversion path, which remains the best default for most models. Reach for the Tensor API when you need low-level control over the graph or want the whole pipeline to run end to end on the accelerator.
The LiteRT Tensor API also serves as an
ideal programmatic foundation for AI coding agents,
providing structured primitives to generate, rewire, and tune model graphs automatically. In the rest of this post, we’ll dive into the design and walk through practical code examples showing how to author models from scratch.
Real-world showcase: Segment Anything on Web
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
To show the Tensor API in practice, we built an interactive
Segment Anything App
, running entirely on-device in the browser on WebGPU. The app enables real-time multi-object segmentation and tracking via Meta's
Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2)
, triggered either by simple clicks or natural language prompts powered by
Gemma 4 E2B
.
The SAM 2 model is fully authored in C++ via the LiteRT Tensor API. A coding agent wrote and evolved it from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU. See that the complete implementation and the web app are open source in the
LiteRT Samples
GitHub repo.
What is the LiteRT Tensor API?
The LiteRT Tensor API provides four key features for authoring and optimizing on-device models:
Full control over graph structure
: you decide every op in the model graph and every connection between them, from elementwise math to accelerator-optimized LLM composite ops, such as scaled dot-product attention, RMSNorm, and KV-cache updates.
Direct weight ingestion
: load weights straight from model checkpoints, such as Hugging Face
.safetensors
files, without conversion scripts needed in between.
Tensor-centric buffer interop
: pre-processing, model partitions, and post-processing pass tensors to each other through shared accelerator buffers, so intermediate data stays on the accelerator with zero copies.
Building blocks for AI agents
: models are plain C++ built from well-defined ops, so coding agents can construct a model, check its results against a reference, and tune its performance by benchmarking variants on each device.
Cross-platform performance
We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder). The SAM 2.1
sample
includes the benchmark commands so you can reproduce the results.
Note: Times cover the image encoder and mask decoder; pre- and post-processing add ~0.34 ms. Output masks match Meta's PyTorch reference pixel for pixel.
Get started with Tensor API
Authoring model in native C++
With the Tensor API, each layer is a C++ function over
Tensor
values, built from high-level operators and weights loaded directly from the checkpoint. For example, here is a multi-head self-attention layer:
// Multi-head self-attention over x: [batch, tokens, dim].
Tensor Attention(const Tensor& x, const WeightMap& w, int heads) {
std::vector<int> s = x.GetShape();
int b = s[0], n = s[1], dim = s[2], d = dim / heads;
Tensor q = FullyConnected(x, w.at("q_proj.weight"), w.at("q_proj.bias"));
Tensor k = FullyConnected(x, w.at("k_proj.weight"), w.at("k_proj.bias"));
Tensor v = FullyConnected(x, w.at("v_proj.weight"), w.at("v_proj.bias"));
// Split heads: [b, n, dim] -> [b, heads, n, d].
q = Transpose(Reshape(q, {b, n, heads, d}), {0, 2, 1, 3});
k = Transpose(Reshape(k, {b, n, heads, d}), {0, 2, 1, 3});
v = Transpose(Reshape(v, {b, n, heads, d}), {0, 2, 1, 3});
// softmax(q * k^T / sqrt(d)) * v, for all heads at once.
Tensor scores = BatchMatMul(q, k, /*adj_x=*/false, /*adj_y=*/true);
Tensor attn = Softmax(Mul(scores, 1.0f / std::sqrt(static_cast<float>(d))));
Tensor out = BatchMatMul(attn, v);
// Merge heads: [b, heads, n, d] -> [b, n, dim], then project.
out = Reshape(Transpose(out, {0, 2, 1, 3}), {b, n, dim});
return FullyConnected(out, w.at("out_proj.weight"), w.at("out_proj.bias"));
}
C
Copied
In the SAM 2 sample,
BuildEncoder
and
BuildDecoder
compose layers like this into the encoder and decoder graphs, and
ModelFactory
exports both as two signatures of one
sam2_image.tflite
file.
A
.tflite
file is one of two ways to run your graph. The backend is a template argument on
Tensor: TfLiteMixinTag
exports a
.tflite
that LiteRT runs on CPU,
ML Drift
(GPU), or NPU, and
XnnpackMixinTag
runs the same code directly on CPU through XNNPACK, with no model file. Tag tensors with both to keep both options:
// Tag tensors for both backends; ops record one graph either can run.
using T = Tensor<TfLiteMixinTag, XnnpackMixinTag>;
T y = Attention(x, w, /*heads=*/8);  // The layer above, over T values.
// Export a .tflite and run it with LiteRT on CPU, GPU, or NPU.
Save({y}, "attention.tflite");
// Or run the same graph directly on the CPU with XNNPACK.
auto runner = XnnpackRunner::Create({y});
runner->Run();
C
Copied
SAM 2 takes the
.tflite
path to reach WebGPU in the browser, and the rest of this post follows it. The
Gemma 4 example
takes the direct path for prefill and decode on CPU, the lightest way to run Tensor API code. The
Tensor API README
walks through both.
A natural workflow uses both: iterate on the direct XNNPACK path, loading weights straight from the
.safetensors
checkpoint with no model file to rebuild, then export a
.tflite
when you're ready to ship with LiteRT on mobile or on the web through LiteRT.js.
Expressing the full ML computation graph
A real app needs more than the neural network itself. In the demo, turning a camera frame and a click into a mask takes four steps: pre-processing converts the frame into the 512x512 image the model expects; the image encoder turns that image into features; the mask decoder combines those features with the click to predict a mask; and post-processing scales the mask back to the frame's size. Running this whole pipeline fast takes two things: keeping data on the accelerator (such as the GPU) between steps, and controlling how each step runs on each accelerator.
Zero copies: Keep the whole pipeline on the accelerator
In a typical app, only the model runs on the GPU; the CPU resizes each camera frame, passes the encoder's output to the decoder, and post-processes the mask. Each trip copies data and stalls the GPU.
In
litert-samples/sam2
, all four steps are Tensor API graphs on the GPU. Pre-processing, for example, is a small graph built with
CreateLambdaRunner
. The graphs are connected once at startup to share buffers, then run for each frame and click:
// Pre-processing is authored with the same Tensor API ops as the model:
// RGBA camera frame [1, H, W, 4] -> normalized pixels [1, 512, 512, 3].
auto pre_runner = CreateLambdaRunner(
env, options,
{{"frame", Tensor({.type = Type::kU8, .shape = {1, H, W, 4}})}},
[=](const TensorsMap& inputs) {
Tensor rgb = Slice(inputs.at("frame"), {0, 0, 0, 0}, {1, H, W, 3});
Tensor resized = ResizeBilinear(Cast(rgb, Type::kFP32), {512, 512});
return TensorsMap{{"pixels", Add(Mul(resized, scale), bias)}};
});
auto model = LitertDynamicRunner::Create(env, "sam2_image.tflite", options);
// Connect once: neighboring steps share buffers, so nothing is copied.
pre_runner.SetOutput("pixels", model.GetInput("encode_image", "pixels"));
for (auto name : {"image_embeddings", "feat_s1", "feat_s0"}) {
model.SetInput("decode_mask", name, model.GetOutput("encode_image", name));
}
post_runner.SetInput("masks", model.GetOutput("decode_mask", "masks"));
C
Copied
No data returns to the CPU between steps: all 522 encoder and 269 decoder operations run on the GPU, and pre- and post-processing add only about 0.34 ms per frame.
Full control: Tune the graph for each backend
Because the graph is plain C++, you or your coding agent can rewrite it for each backend. Our agent,
Antigravity
, moved SAM 2's per-frame decisions, such as whether the object is still visible, from CPU code into the graph. Comparisons like score > 0 would still fall back to the CPU on WebGPU, because they output true/false values, so the agent rewrote them as arithmetic in
StepPos
:
// Simplified from StepPos and BuildStep in sam2v_graph.cc.
// Before: Greater outputs true/false values, which fall back to the CPU.
// Tensor visible = Cast(Greater(score, zero), Type::kFP32);
// After: GPU-friendly ops; 0 for score <= 0, 1 for score >= 1e-4.
Tensor visible = Sub(1.0f, Relu(Sub(1.0f, Mul(Relu(score), 1e4f))));
// Keep the mask if the object is visible; otherwise, blank it out.
Tensor mask = Add(Mul(best_mask, visible), Mul(Sub(1.0f, visible), -1024.0f));
C
Copied
Each object now takes a single GPU call per frame. The agent made a series of changes like this, such as folding the attention scale into the weights, and checked each against Hugging Face's SAM 2 before keeping it. That's how we more than tripled the model's frame rate.
What's next
We're working on direct
ML Drift
(GPU) backends, NPU-friendly operations, and automatic full-graph quantization. We're also adding Python authoring with
.tflite
export, plus wider dynamic-shape support for varying image sizes, batch sizes, and sequence lengths.
