items.title: Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes The google/adk-recipes repository unifies Agent Development Kit (ADK) resources into three structured layers—core/, plugins/, a
items.content:
Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes
- Google Developers Blog
Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes
OCT. 15, 2026
Pier Paolo Ippolito
Product Manager
Shahin Saadati
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
The curated library of ADK recipes powering Google Cloud's Agents CLI, Agent Garden, and Gemini Enterprise app.
Introduction
A developer building on Google Cloud today can scaffold a long-horizon memory agent from the terminal, install a retail vertical skill into a coding assistant with one line, and deploy a fully-wired production service to Cloud Run, Agent Runtime, Agent Garden, or Gemini Enterprise app — all from the same curated source tree. That tree is
google/adk-recipes
, the restructured successor to
google/adk-samples
that now serves Agent Platform from a single source of truth.
ADK recipes are agent-friendly: we've made it easy for your agents to 1) discover relevant recipes for various agent use cases, and 2) install and use them automatically from your favorite harness.
google/adk-recipes
splits its content into three top-level folders:
core/
for reference patterns curated by the Agents CLI and DevRel teams, plugins/ for installable vertical skills packaged as Plugin Recipes conforming to the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 spec, and contrib/ for end-to-end deployable services across five languages. Every piece has been designed with machine readability as the primary consideration.
What follows is a walkthrough of the
repository
's shape, three worked examples (one per layer), and a reflection on what the new structure enables.
What's in the repo
Three top-level roots, each anchored on one reader action:
Every recipe ships a validated
manifest.yaml
, an
AGENTS.md
that tells the coding assistant opening it what the recipe is and how to use it, and (for
contrib/
and
plugins/
) a
Dockerfile
plus a runnability test. CI enforces the standards on every PR, and a suite of coding-assistant skills in the repo (
prepare-python-recipe
,
generate-manifest
,
github-pr-review
, and others) does most of the preparation, so your agent can scaffold, validate, and submit a recipe end-to-end.
Built for coding assistants, not just developers
Every
AGENTS.md
, every
manifest.yaml
, every
SKILL.md
is written primarily for the AI coding assistant that will open the repo on your behalf;
README.md
files are what humans still read. The handbook glossary captures the dual framing:
"Recipe — a runnable agent example (or importable agent module) under
core/
,
contrib/
, or
plugins/
, consumed by ADK developers and coding agents alike."
What it powers across the Agent Platform
adk-recipes
serves as the single source of truth for ADK content across the three Agent Platform surfaces that consume it. Each reads the repository through its own protocol.
Agents CLI reads
core/
. When a developer runs
uvx --from google-agents-cli agents-cli create my-agent
, Agents CLI can scaffold on demand a
core/
recipe. The CLI, launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next, exposes the full scaffold → deploy → evaluate → publish lifecycle; the base content it serves comes from our recipes. Horizon, the reference harness we examine below, is an example pattern Agents CLI treats as a production template.
Agent Garden features a curated selection. The developer-facing path into the repository is a pull request to
contrib/
: a recipe lands in GitHub, becomes part of the public ADK ecosystem, and from that moment is discoverable by other developers and by coding assistants reading the repository. Appearing in the Agent Garden gallery is a separate editorial decision made by the Agent Garden team, which curates a subset of recipes and promotes them to the public catalog on their own cadence. Once an agent is in the gallery, any developer in a Google Cloud project gets a one-click install.
Beyond these primary surfaces, Google Cloud's own infrastructure components appear as building blocks inside the recipes themselves. Horizon uses Agent Platform Sandboxes for per-user sandboxing, Memory Bank for durable memory, and Agent Platform Sessions for session state. The retail product-search Plugin Recipe uses Vector Search 2.0 on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform paired with BigQuery. The retail virtual-tryon Plugin Recipe uses Gemini image models for still composites and Veo 3.1 Reference-to-Video for animated outputs. The recipes do not just live alongside Agent Platform; they document it in use.
For developers working with coding assistants outside Google Cloud's tooling (Claude Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and others), Plugin Recipes additionally install through the open
npx skills
CLI maintained by vercel-labs.
Horizon: a reference pattern for
core/
Building an agent that can handle a single conversation is a well-understood problem. Building one that holds its own across days of interaction, remembering what the user did yesterday and planning tasks for tomorrow, is a materially different undertaking. The hard parts of such a long-horizon system are the same regardless of what the agent is being built to do: cross-session memory, per-user sandboxing of tool execution, secrets management, guardrails against runaway behaviour, and the orchestration primitives that make multi-step tasks resumable. Horizon, which lives at
core/python/long-horizon-harness
, is the reference harness we built to collect these primitives in one place.
The shortest path from a fresh clone to a running Horizon instance:
uvx google-agents-cli setup
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/google/adk-recipes.git
cd adk-recipes
git sparse-checkout set core/python/long-horizon-harness
cd core/python/long-horizon-harness
# Default: LHA_ENVIRONMENT_BACKEND=local, in-memory sessions, no cloud deploys needed
make dev-local
Plain text
Copied
make deploy
rolls the backend to Cloud Run through Terraform; make destroy tears it back down. Horizon's evaluation suite lives in
tests/eval/evalsets/
as eighteen named behavioural rubrics covering memory recall, injection-based exfiltration attempts, guardrail halting under adversarial input, tool-selection discipline, and a journey-level plot-artifact evaluation. The rubrics are executed with
uv run pytest tests/eval
.
A first chat turn against the running backend confirms the memory layer is wired correctly:
Horizon is the harness we give coding assistants to study before building something harder. When a developer asks their assistant to build an agent that must run across days of interaction, the right next step is
uvx google-agents-cli create
with Horizon as the scaffold, and the rest of the harness falls into place.
The retail Plugin Recipe
Horizon encodes a reference pattern. It does not encode a vertical. For that, the second layer of the repository holds Plugin Recipes, each addressing a specific industry domain. The first vertical fully covered in this launch is retail, available under
plugins/retail/
.
The Plugin Recipe format sits on top of the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 specification published at
agent-plugins.org
, an open standard for packaging installable AI skills across coding assistants. The specification defines a plugin as a bundle of one or more skills with a top-level
plugin.json
manifest declaring name, version, license, and ownership. Each skill is a self-contained folder with a
SKILL.md
conversational installer, a
README.md
, an
EVAL.yaml
of quality gates, and the scripts and assets the skill needs to do its work. The retail plugin's layout is:
plugins/retail/
├── plugin.json
└── skills/
├── product-search/
│   ├── SKILL.md       # Q-MODE conversational installer
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── EVAL.yaml      # LLM-as-judge rubrics + deterministic assertions
│   ├── scripts/
│   ├── references/
│   └── assets/
└── virtual-tryon/
└── ...
Plain text
Copied
Two skills ship in this plugin today. The first,
retail-product-search
, builds an ADK agent with a vector-search retrieval tool backed by Vector Search 2.0 on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and a BigQuery catalog. The skill handles the entire pipeline: ingesting a CSV or JSON catalog into BigQuery, generating multimodal and text embeddings with Vertex AI Embeddings, building the Vector Search collection, scaffolding the ADK agent with a
retrieve_docs
tool, and deploying to Cloud Run. The agent is deliberately single-agent: one
root_agent
with one retrieval tool and no coordinator layer. The semantic complexity sits in the retrieval pipeline and the evaluator rubric, not in agent-to-agent communication; adding orchestration layers would obscure the pattern rather than clarify it.
The second skill,
retail-virtual-tryon
, generates a photorealistic composite of a model wearing or holding a product, with an optional eight-second studio catwalk video on top. It uses
gemini-2.5-flash-image
by default, falling back to
gemini-2.5-pro-image
when editorial quality matters more than latency. For video it uses
veo-3.1-generate-001
in Reference-to-Video mode, conditioning the generated motion on the still produced by the image pipeline. The skill ships a pre-flight product-cutout classifier and configurable safety levels, operational details that become obvious after the third real production deployment.
Both skills install into any coding assistant that reads skills with a single command:
# From Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor …
npx skills add google/adk-recipes --skill retail-product-search --full-depth
npx skills add google/adk-recipes --skill retail-virtual-tryon --full-depth
Plain text
Copied
The
--full-depth
flag instructs the CLI to walk past its default top-level lookup and discover the nested
plugins/retail/skills/
structure. The install lands in
~/.agents/skills/<skill-name>/
and is symlinked into every detected coding assistant on the local machine:
$ npx skills add google/adk-recipes --skill retail-product-search --full-depth -g
●  claude-code_2-1-288_agent  Agent detected — installing non-interactively
◇  Source: https://github.com/google/adk-recipes.git
◇  Repository cloned
◇  Found 11 skills
●  Installing to: Antigravity CLI, Augment, IBM Bob, Claude Code, OpenClaw,
CodeBuddy, Continue, Crush, Droid, Goose, Junie, iFlow CLI,
Kilo Code, Kiro CLI, Kode, MCPJam, Mux, OpenHands, Qoder, Qwen Code,
Roo Code, Trae, Windsurf, Zencoder, …
◇  Installation Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  ~/.agents/skills/retail-product-search                                │
│    universal: Antigravity CLI, Droid, Kilo Code, Amp +15   │
│    symlink → Augment, IBM Bob, Claude Code, OpenClaw, CodeBuddy +25    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
◇  Installed 1 skill
└  Done!  Review skills before use; they run with full agent permissions.
Plain text
Copied
The skill ecosystem is designed to compose. The
retail-product-search SKILL.md
instructs the host coding assistant to pull two companion skills from
google/skills
if they are not already installed, keeping cross-cutting concerns like BigQuery basics and Gemini API usage in one place and reusable by multiple vertical plugins.
Once installed, the coding assistant reads
SKILL.md
and initiates a Q-MODE interview. For
retail-product-search
, Quick Start is two questions (GCP project ID and the path to product data, with sensible defaults for both); Full Setup adds two more covering product-fields level and GCP region. By the end of the interview the skill has written a
./design-spec.md
reflecting the project's actual shape and executed
scripts/setup.py
to land the catalog in BigQuery, generate the embeddings, build the Vector Search collection, and run
EVAL.yaml
against the result. If the rubric and assertion checks fall below the 80 percent passing target, the skill halts and surfaces the specific failures.
An end-to-end setup run on the bundled five-product demo catalog produces:
$ .venv/bin/python scripts/setup.py --config ./design-spec.md
INFO:__main__: SETUP PIPELINE (driven by design-spec.md)
INFO:__main__:   Project:      testproject-425813
INFO:__main__:   Region:       us-central1
INFO:__main__:   Validating sample data... Validated 5 records.
INFO:__main__:   Ingesting into BigQuery...
INFO:ingest_bigquery: Creating dataset testproject-425813.retail_skill_products
INFO:ingest_bigquery: Loaded 5 valid products
INFO:__main__:   Creating Vector Search collection...
INFO:ingest_vertex_search: Collection created successfully
INFO:ingest_vertex_search: Ingestion complete: 5 created, 0 skipped, 0 errors
INFO:__main__: SETUP COMPLETE
Plain text
Copied
A live retrieval against the collection the skill has just provisioned returns:
>>> from app.agent import retrieve_docs
>>> retrieve_docs("wireless headphones under 200")

Thinking
Summary
Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.
Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.
Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.
Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)
Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.
Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.
Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.
Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.
Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.
Benchmark Results
We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.
GIFT-Eval - GMean MASE
GIFT-Eval - GMean WQL
GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.
TIME - GMean MASE
TIME - GMean CRPS
TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.
fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.
Family of models optimised for every specification
Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.
Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.
Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.
An industrial example
Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.
Multivariate forecasting.
A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.
Probabilistic forecasting.
A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.
Categorical covariates.
Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.
Known-future covariates.
Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.
From Model to System
Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.
In the plant, that could look like this:
Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.
When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.
The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.
The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.
The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.
Key technical contributions
Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.
Decoupled Horizon Forecasting.
Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.
Covariate-aware attention.
Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.
Synthetic-first data.
The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.
Two-stage training.
Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.
A model that can be adapted
Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.
For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through
Mistral Forge
, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:
Zero-shot inference
out of the box.
Architectural extensions
, such as domain-specific covariates.
Fine-tuning on proprietary data
, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.
Control over the training data
, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.
The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.
What’s next
We have published a
GitHub repository
so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
See a demo
Try Perplexity
Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
Perplexity open-sources SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer, to help developers build safer autonomous AI agents
Oct 15, 2026
Since launching
Computer
in February, Perplexity has been an early pioneer in personal agents. Weâre committed to the hard problems of agent governance, detecting unsafe behaviors and preventing rogue agent activity. In July, we replaced our commercially available sandbox provider with a more robust and resilient in-house solution we named
SPACE
.
SPACE provides high security for advanced agentic systems. In fact, a recent
barrage of security testing
proved SPACE resilient against network-bypass techniques like those used in the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident.
Today, we're open-sourcing SPACE to give developers a foundation for building safer agent systems and contributing to stronger protections across the industry. Developers can access the
repository here
.
Agent governance is an engineering problem
, and open source is essential to solving it. When developers have systems they can inspect, adapt, and build on, they find more weaknesses and develop better tools. Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a production-tested foundation for agent runtimes, with isolation, state recovery, and credential and network controls built in.
Creating a foundation for other builders
Sandboxes keep agents secure, letting them access the tools and files they need to complete these tasks, while keeping sensitive information protected.
Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a starting point for the environments where their agents run code and work with files. Teams can see how the SPACE sandbox platform works and build on its implementation. They can also adapt it to their needs rather than recreating the underlying infrastructure.
In Computer, SPACE supports isolated code execution, pause and resume, recovery, and session branching. Those capabilities provide the foundation for assistants that could:
Analyze data:
Clean a spreadsheet, run calculations, and create charts in a separate workspace.
Resume work:
Pause for someone to review a draft or supply missing information, then resume with their files and running state preserved.
Explore alternatives:
Test two ways to clean a dataset in separate copies of their workspace, or restore an earlier file after a mistake.
These examples illustrate how developers could use SPACE's documented isolation and session controls. Platform and security engineers can also review the isolation model and security examples before integrating SPACE into their own systems.
Increasing security for autonomous work
When we give agents more room to solve problems, we need
clear limits
on how they do it. We know that agents pursuing legitimate tasks can still cross security boundaries when they attempt to work around missing files, failed requests, or permission denials.
We can put model safeguards into place to reduce the likelihood of unsafe behavior. Adding independent controls in the surrounding system helps contain the damage if those safeguards fail. They limit what an agent can access regardless of what it decides to do.
SPACE puts those controls around a separate workspace for agent-generated code and files. We designed it to combine isolation, recovery, and efficient execution. This lets agents perform useful work over long sessions without relying on the model alone to respect security boundaries.
Running inside its own operating system
Each SPACE sandbox runs inside a small virtual machine with its own operating system, creating an isolation boundary between the agentâs work and the host system. A central control plane coordinates when these workspaces are created, paused, resumed, or removed.
SPACE treats the sandbox as untrusted and manages network access and platform-held credentials outside the sandbox. Agents can connect to authorized services without those credentials being stored in their working environment.
Frequent file snapshots
and checkpoints of the full running environment preserve progress across interruptions. To keep these operations efficient, SPACE stores changes rather than repeatedly copying entire environments. This reduces the work needed to create, restore, or branch a sandbox.
Improving production performance
Since July, SPACE has powered all Computer sessions and has handled millions of sandbox creations per day.
In a comparison
on the same production traffic, sandbox creation was three to five times faster than with our previous provider.
We also
tested SPACE
against agents deliberately trying to breach its boundaries. Our published security evaluation found no escape from the virtual machine to the host in 108 attempts, but some found ways around network restrictions. We fixed those weaknesses, and neither identified attack method succeeded in follow-up testing.
We also disclosed related weaknesses we found in other sandbox platforms to their vendors, extending that work beyond our own infrastructure.
Contributing to safer agentic AI
SPACE is part of a broader effort to strengthen the systems people rely on as AI takes on more work. Through the
Secure Intelligence Institute
, we conduct security research and collaborate with the wider community, translating findings into practical defenses.
We believe open-sourcing security tools gives developers more ways to test defenses, find weaknesses, and build safer AI systems. We've shared tools that address different parts of that work:
BrowseSafe
, a model and benchmark for detecting malicious instructions hidden in web pages.
Numbat
, a security toolkit, open-sourced in July, that helps detect, investigate, and prevent dangerous agent behavior on computers
Bumblebee
, a scanner open-sourced in May, that checks developer machines for risky software packages, extensions, and AI tool configurations
Making these tools available lets other teams inspect our work, adapt it to their needs, and contribute improvements. With SPACE, we're extending that approach to the environments where agents execute code and work with files.
Deploying for agent systems
Akamai
has tested and launched SPACE on its cloud platform and is working with Perplexity to bring it to its customers.
Crusoe
is also partnering with Perplexity to add SPACE to its Managed AI Services portfolio.
CoreWeave
has published setup guidance for developers who want to deploy SPACE for evaluation on
CKS
.
Developers can start with the SPACEâs setup instructions and security guidance to deploy it for their own agent systems. The
repository
and
documentation
define the supported configurations and included components.

Rollouts and Security Review
Today we're launching two Cursor bots for the last mile of shipping code. Rollouts watches every change as it deploys and reports its health per environment. Security Review reports exploitable bugs on every pull request.
Both are available today on Teams and Enterprise plans.
#
Rollouts
Rollouts attaches a monitor to every pull request and watches the change as it deploys, reporting change health per environment: verified healthy, regression detected, or inconclusive. It's the Cursor version of
Firetiger
Change Monitors, rebuilt with the Bot Development Kit.
Enable it from the dashboard and connect source control, your deploy system, and your telemetry provider. Rollouts starts watching on the next pull request.
#
Monitoring plans
When a pull request opens, Rollouts reads the diff and the systems it touches, then writes a monitoring plan as a PR comment. The plan lists the risks it identified, the effect the change is meant to have, the signals it will check, and any gaps in instrumentation that would make the change hard to verify. Edit the plan in the PR and Rollouts uses your version.
#
Deploy tracking
Rollouts wakes on deploy events for the change's commit and runs the plan against your logs, metrics, and traces. It tracks each environment separately, so a change can be verified in staging and still flagged in production. Rollouts checks the change's intended effect alongside error and latency signals, and reports back on the PR when it reaches a verdict.
#
Regressions
When Rollouts detects a regression, it names the change it suspects and notifies the author. Depending on configuration, it can also open a revert PR for review or hand the finding to a cloud agent for a fix. Rollouts does not merge or roll back on its own today.
#
Integrations
Rollouts connects to Origin or GitHub for source control, to your continuous delivery system for deploy events, and to Datadog and other telemetry providers for signals. Feature flag integration is coming soon.
#
Security Review
Security Review is available today. It reads every pull request in the context of the codebase and posts one review comment reporting exploitable bugs. Style and quality stay with Bugbot.
Enable it from the dashboard for the repositories you want reviewed. Draft PRs are skipped.
#
What it reports
Security Review looks for injection across SQL, command, and template surfaces, along with authentication and authorization bypasses, including checks that a refactor stopped running. It also flags secrets and credentials committed to source, SSRF and unvalidated redirects, unsafe deserialization, and dependency changes that introduce known vulnerabilities. It traces where user input enters and what it passes through.
#
Findings
Each finding carries a severity, the attack path, and a proposed fix. Dismiss one with a reason and Security Review won't raise it again on that PR.
#
Team rules
Add rules for your codebase, such as which client external calls must go through or which tables are never queried from a request handler, and Security Review enforces them on every PR.
#
Get started
Rollouts and Security Reviewer are available today on Teams and Enterprise plans. Enable either bot from the
automations
tab.
For the next 10 days, we're including usage credits so teams can try Rollouts on real changes. Teams and Enterprise customers receive credits for roughly 50 and 500 changes, respectively.

Today we're launching Projects in Cursor. Projects lets you take on larger bodies of work, such as a feature, a migration, or a full app. It maintains context over months of work, delegates tasks to thousands of subagents, and performs recurring work without being prompted.
Access Projects from the left-hand nav. The coordinator agent in a project doesn't write code itself; it plans the work, delegates it to agents that implement it, and brings the finished work back to you to check. Coordinators create and manage agents on your behalf, running as many in parallel as the work needs.

Powered by Cloud Agents
A Project runs on its own computer in the cloud, so closing your laptop doesn't stop it. When something needs testing on your machine, the coordinator spins up a local agent to run it there.
#
Shared context
You shouldn't have to onboard an agent every time you start a task. Each Project maintains a set of files that sync across every cloud and local machine its agents use. Agents add research and artifacts, along with what they learn about the codebase and how you prefer work to be done. If one agent figures out how to test a service, for example, every future agent can use those instructions. The shared context grows with the Project, making the coordinator more effective over time.
#
Subscriptions
Tell the coordinator agent to watch a Slack channel, run on a schedule, or follow all your PRs. This way it can take action based on signals it detects, without waiting for your prompt.
Connect Slack and point it at a bug-report channel, and it starts delegating each time a bug comes in.

Today, we're releasing North Small Translate, a mixture-of-experts machine translation model with strong performance across 50+ languages. Across WMT26 benchmarks,¹ North Small Translate achieves an 83.6 score across all languages, outperforming proprietary models like DeepL and Google Translate, as well as open-weight alternatives such as Gemma 4 31B (off), GLM 5.2, and Mistral Large 3.
North Small Translate marks a significant milestone as Cohere's first translation model in the North model family. It builds on our multilingual and translation lineage — from the
Tiny Aya model family
to
Command A Translate
— and represents a clear next step in Cohere’s commitment to offering high-quality machine translation wherever it is needed.
Now available for research and non-commercial use under a
CC BY-NC 4.0
license, North Small Translate advances Cohere’s mission to make sovereign AI a technological reality.
Visit
Hugging Face
to download the weights - available in several near-lossless quantizations - explore our
HuggingFace space
to demo the model, and read our
implementation guides
.

Leading translation quality in the open ecosystem
North Small Translate outperforms similarly sized open-weight models under 1T parameters and API-based translation models in various dimensions of machine translation on average. In WMT model evaluations, North Small Translate leads with an WMT26 All Languages benchmark score of 83.60, compared with 81.56 for Qwen 3.5 397B A17B, 76.50 for GLM 5.2 FP8, 81.37 for DeepL NextGen, 79.46 for Gemma 4 31B (on), and 68.20 for Google Translate. North Small Translate (Agentic) — which can find errors and fix errors in translation — scores even higher, at 84.36.²
Image 1: Overall WMT26 scores across all languages across major models, benchmarked for WMT 2026 using GPT-5.6-Sol as a judge.
North Small Translate performs strongly across 32 high-resource languages and 18 additional languages. North Small Translate is the most consistent performer across the full spread of regions, without the sharp regional drop-offs seen in other models of its size. On average across all languages, it is the best-performing dedicated machine translation model in this evaluation — open or closed.
Image 2: Overall WMT scores by regional average across DeepL, Google Translate, and Gemma 31B (on), and North Small Translate using GPT-5.6-Sol as a judge.
At the regional level, North Small Translate punches above its weight, beating Gemma 4 31B (on) outright in Europe (82.2 vs. 73.9) while running essentially even with it in South Asia (86.2 vs. 86.7).
At the regional level, both North Small Translate and its Agentic counterpart beat Gemma 4 31B (on) outright across Europe — EU languages (82.74 Agentic / 82.17 standard vs. 72.73) and non-EU European languages (81.52 / 81.24 vs. 75.90) — while running essentially even with it in South Asia (87.13 / 86.16 vs. 88.04).
Both versions also outperform DeepL NextGen across every non-European region tested — MENA, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and East Asia — with the largest advantage in South Asia and MENA (roughly 8–10 points ahead of DeepL), a moderate edge in Southeast Asia (about 4–5 points), and the narrowest edge in East Asia (about 1-3 points, with the standard model closing in on DeepL's 85.41 score).
Increased throughput for faster workflows
North Small Translate is built for high-throughput generation, prioritizing raw output speed even as concurrency scales.
In our testing, North Small Translate achieved up to 1.4x higher output throughput than Gemma 4 31B TP1 (1 x GPU) under identical concurrency levels and hardware configurations — 112 vs. 81 Output Tokens per Second (TOPS) at low concurrency and 39 vs. 30 TOPS at high concurrency. In practical terms, that's 30-38% more tokens generated per second, translating to meaningfully faster completion times on longer outputs.
Image 3: North Small Translate’s output speed compared to Gemma 4 31B (off), across high and low concurrencies, in internal tests on identical hardware.
Long documents are where many translation models fall apart, and North Small Translate isn't one of them. It scores 48.9 on our long-context evaluation, more than double Google Translate (21.3) and Gemma 4 31B (19.4), and ahead of every general-purpose LLM we tested.³
Paired with its throughput advantage, that means fast, reliable translation at length, without the quality collapse seen in most non-specialized alternatives.
Efficient cost of translation, at scale
Efficiency is a core constraint in enterprise translation deployment, and we engineered North Small Translate to be extremely cost-efficient, without sacrificing performance.
Image 4: Overall WMT score and cost per task breakdown across machine translation models, using pricing per token or character from model providers' websites.
For enterprises evaluating commercial licenses of North Small Translate, benefit from a strong 80.1 score at just $0.000676 per task, using only 661 tokens on average. Compared to Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (high) — which costs $0.038928 per task (5,762% more than North Small Translate).
Similarly sized models like Qwen 3.5 397B A17B and Cohere’s own Command A+ have decent performance at $0.004525 and $0.005158 per task, respectively.
Best in translation, in partnership with RWS
North Small Translate was developed in partnership with
RWS
, an AI solutions company pioneering in language technology and services. Close collaboration with RWS, specifically Language Weaver’s research and science teams along with its language experts, helped shape the model's real-world translation performance throughout development. RWS works with more than 80% of the world’s top 100 brands, empowering the world's most ambitious brands to communicate seamlessly across borders and cultures.
For enterprises that need more than open-weight research access, security, scalability, and a dedicated translation and localization platform, North Small Translate, is available through RWS’s
Language Weaver
product.
Getting Started
North Small Translate is available today on
Hugging Face
for non-commercial and research use. Visit our
documentation
for detailed model specs, deployment guides, and implementation examples to get started. For information about how the model was developed, read our
technical report

Posts tagged "AI" All posts tagged with AI https://blog.cloudflare.com/tag/ai/ en-us https://blog.cloudflare.com/favicon.ico Cloudflare Blog https://blog.cloudflare.com Tue, 20 Oct 2026 06:16:16 GMT Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization https://blog.cloudflare.com/obsessive-inference-optimization/ Mon, 19 Oct 2026 19:12:53 GMT When our AI code reviewer's cost per run doubled, we dug into the token usage to find out why. Learn how we used prompt caching and intelligent model routing to slash our inference bill by 68% while speeding up reviews. Ryan Skidmore Agents AI Durable Objects

When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April, an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave.

Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before.

About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in.

How a review doubled in cost

The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data.

The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though.

At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models.

Our internal standards reviewer, Codex, ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself.

The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost.

What else has changed since our last post?

One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out!

So, where were the tokens going?

Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%,  cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that  most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again.

That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both.

It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it.

That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls.

Sharing a cached prefix between every repository

Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider.

The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits.

The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written.

On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs.

The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72.

Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release.

Fewer calls, fewer dollars

The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review.

Change

What was happening

Effect of change

Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use

Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering.

One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request

Reading files in parallel

In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file.

Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB

Skipping reviewers on re-reviews

About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at.

On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%.

Stopping after the review is posted

OpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw.

About $0.07 saved per job

Treating a slow reviewer differently from a broken provider

A reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit.

Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost none

Canceling canceled jobs

GitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished.

Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelled

The most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it.

A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer.

Changing models and effort

The next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked.

When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving.

Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment.

The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings.

Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%.

The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5.

On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below.

To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that.

Latency

We weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers.

The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30.

By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been.

Review quality

A cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened.

With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions.

First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence.

Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews.

Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low.

Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical.

So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next.

Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems.

Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%.

Where this leaves us

An average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each session’s first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside.

Lower cost reviews didn’t automatically mean worse quality, but it didn’t automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level you’re paying for.

If you’re at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, I’m talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, It’s time to build, not buy, on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. I’ll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.

01M58NMKW6A1DQJNZXH37VZ9JH Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models https://blog.cloudflare.com/clairic-extraction-model/ Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:48:26 GMT Clairic is a new model from Cloudflare that is a System One extraction modeI, capable of extracting, computing, estimating, and forecasting data from unstructured inputs. Alex Reneau Michelle Chen Kevin Flansburg AI Developers Machine Learning Research Workers AI

Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs.

Context

When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows.

We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models.

Introducing System One extraction models

Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it.

Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds.

An extraction model can return:

  • Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score.
  • Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score.
  • Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval.
  • Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval.

And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look.

Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models:

System One: Extract

System One: Decide

System Two

Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words.

How a request works

Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases.

A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap.

Type

Returns

text

A specific span of the input, with its offsets

number

A number read or computed, honoring integer and decimals

date, time, datetime

Calendar dates and valid times, in ISO form

duration

A length of time in the unit you choose

list

Matching text, number or date, in input order

estimate

A distribution inside your [min, max], on your step grid, linear or log scale.

forecast

One estimate per future step of a series

Every scalar answer comes with p_null (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and confidence. Every estimate answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (p10 to p90), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers.

Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs.

An example: Extracting values

Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document.

Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get:

  • Values extracted from your input, so an answer is grounded.
  • Computed values, so it can parse through unstructured data without pre-sanitizing it.
  • Character offset spans, so you can reference where in the input the data was.
  • Confidence labels, so you can determine which values need a second look.
  • A strongly typed output, so numbers and dates are formed under the rules of their type (e.g., a cents field has two decimals).
  • Handling for null values, where a missing field returns with null as an answer (along with an estimated probability of null and a guess).
  • Cheaper and faster answers, because every field is answered in the same parallel pass. So asking for thirty fields costs about the same as asking for three.

Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email:

Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana

From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
state: email,
fields: {
order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
delivered_on:        { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" },
amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
tracking_number:     { type: "text" },
},
});

Clairic returns the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score:

{
"order_id": {
"type": "text",
"p_null": 3.4e-6,
"span": [10, 17],
"guess": "A-88412",
"confidence": 0.999957,
"value": "A-88412"
},
"delivered_on": {
"type": "date",
"p_null": 6.5e-8,
"guess": "2026-09-28",
"confidence": 0.999999,
"value": "2026-09-28"
},
"amount_paid": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 1.6e-5,
"guess": 701.1,
"confidence": 0.999944,
"value": 701.1
},
"days_since_delivery": {
"type": "duration",
"p_null": 6.1e-9,
"unit": "days",
"guess": 11,
"confidence": 0.999999,
"value": 11
},
"damage": {
"type": "list",
"value": ["cracked screen", "dented corner"],
"spans": [[50, 64], [71, 84]]
},
"tracking_number": {
"type": "text",
"p_null": 1,
"span": [106, 112],
"guess": "$52.10",
"confidence": 0.416016,
"value": null
}
}

A few things to notice:

  • amount_paid isn't written anywhere in the email. In this example, Clairic added the price and the tax in the same pass and returns the sum.
  • days_since_delivery is also worked out from two dates in the text, not directly in the input.
  • damage lists both kinds of damage as exact spans, so you can highlight them in the source.
  • tracking_number isn't in the email, so it comes back null instead of a plausible-looking guess. guess shows what the model would otherwise have picked.

Clairic also works with images

Here’s a real-life photo of a receipt — the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesn’t help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract:

{
"model": "clairic",
"answers": {
"order_number": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 0.0040206750854849815,
"guess": 77245,
"confidence": 0.776249383996532,
"value": 77245
},
"purchased_at": {
"type": "datetime",
"p_null": 4.136094133855295e-08,
"guess": "2026-07-01T13:34:00",
"confidence": 0.831464227002992,
"value": "2026-07-01T13:34:00"
},
"quantity": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 5.2313655629632194e-08,
"guess": 2,
"confidence": 0.9997007500403496,
"value": 2
},
"unit_price": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 0.001599092734977603,
"guess": 7.99,
"confidence": 0.9991279019989127,
"value": 7.99
},
"subtotal": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 9.69956488461321e-08,
"guess": 15.98,
"confidence": 0.9999881983893096,
"value": 15.98
},
"sales_tax": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 2.5511653802823275e-06,
"guess": 0,
"confidence": 0.9999800924450729,
"value": 0
},
"tip": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 5.953857908025384e-05,
"guess": 2.39,
"confidence": 0.9335768781214697,
"value": 2.39
},
"discount": {
"type": "number",
"p_null": 0.9994148015975952,
"guess": 0,
"confidence": 0.91852733929319,
"value": null
}
}
}

As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null.

An example: Estimating values

Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances. It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs.

A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100–500", …), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process.

Clairic returns a distribution over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check.

Here’s another example, where Clairic looks at historical home prices and comparable sales, to determine an estimate :

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
state: `Comparable sales:
sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood,sale_price
1450,3,1998,Elm Park,412000
2100,4,2006,Elm Park,585000
980,2,1975,Riverside,265000
1600,3,2003,Elm Park,449000
1300,3,1990,Riverside,318000
Subject property:
sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood
1620,3,2001,Elm Park`,
fields: {
sale_price:     { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 50000, max: 5000000, scale: "log", step: 1000 }
});

Clairic will return an estimated value:

{
"sale_price":     { "type": "estimate", "value": 418000, "median": 415000, "p10": 370000, "p90": 470000, "p_below": 0.0, "p_above": 0.0 }
}

Values always fall inside your bounds, and the width of the interval shows how much the input informs the prediction: price is narrow ($370,000-$470,000), days on market is wide (24-148). Because fields are unlimited and answered in parallel, you can score many items in one call (one estimate per candidate, lead, or listing) and sort them in code.

An example: Forecasting values

Forecasting values in a time series is quite hard for generalized models — it usually means you have to either build a specific pipeline per metric (parse the data, fit a model, tune it, deploy it), or you paste 36 months of numbers into an LLM and ask for the next three. The first is accurate but really expensive and time-consuming to set up for every new series. The second is easy, but you get point forecasts with no intervals, forecasts that shift depending on how the prompt is worded, and answers with limited confidence.

Clairic sits between the two — it is not claiming to replace a dedicated time-series model, but it is a little faster and cheaper than your regular LLM. A forecast field takes the history as plain text in state and returns, for every step ahead, a value and an 80% interval, inside the bounds you declare. It reads the history the way you already have it, whether that's a CSV export, a pasted dashboard, or rows mixed with notes, and may often work with no need to clean up your data beforehand.

To see how that holds up on real data, we used a public series: the number of people the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens at U.S. airport checkpoints each day. Each morning we asked Clairic for the next day's count, given the real counts so far, for 21 days in a row:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
state: `Daily number of people screened at TSA checkpoints at US airports.
date,weekday,travelers
2026-07-16,Thu,2850229
...
2026-10-13,Tue,2353356
Forecast date: 2026-10-14 (Wed)`,
fields: {
travelers: { type: "forecast", horizon: 1, interval: "day",
min: 500000, max: 4000000, scale: "log",
instructions: "Number of people screened tomorrow" },
},
});

Which returns:

{
"travelers": { "type": "forecast", "value": [2416117], "median": [2419283], "p10": [2270774], "p90": [2556769] }
}

In actuality, TSA screened 2,419,474 people that day, which is right around the median 2,419,283 that Clairic predicted.

Data: TSA checkpoint travel numbers, accessed Oct. 15, 2026.

Across the 21 days, Clairic's forecasts were off by 3.3% on average, and 17 of the 21 actual counts landed inside its 80% interval, which follows what an 80% interval should do. It picked up the weekly rhythm from the numbers alone: quieter Tuesdays and Saturdays, busier Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays.

The misses are also interesting: three of the four days outside the interval fall on the Columbus Day weekend, when more people flew than the previous weeks suggested. Clairic forecasts from the patterns in the series but doesn't account for events the series doesn't show, like holidays.

Thinking fast and slow

These models are designed to fit alongside your existing agentic workflows. An extraction model predicts values, a decision model decides what to do with these values, and an LLM takes action with them. It is a perfect marriage between System One and System Two models. It bridges the existing gap, where you either have to manually extract data for LLMs, or have an LLM parse through messy data (which is costly, time-consuming, and can lead to hallucinations). With System One extraction models, you can work with real-world data with more speed, efficiency, and precision.

Here's an example of the damaged-product claim from earlier, illustrating how all the models can work together.  We built this into a live demo you can try here.

// 1. Clairic turns the email into values
const facts = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
state: email,
fields: {
customer_name:       { type: "text", instructions: "Customer's first name" },
order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
repair_cost:         { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 10, max: 5000, scale: "log", step: 1,
instructions: "Cost to repair the damage described" },
},
})).answers;
const { customer_name, order_id, amount_paid, days_since_delivery, damage, repair_cost } = facts;
// 2. Clef decides from Clairic's values and the policy, not from the raw email
const options = {
refund:  "Full refund of the amount paid",
repair:  "Free repair, with a prepaid shipping label",
};
const { choice } = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", {
state: `Damage claim for order ${order_id.value}.
Paid: $${amount_paid.value.toFixed(2)}. Delivered ${days_since_delivery.value} days ago.
Damage reported: ${damage.value.join(", ")}.
Estimated repair cost: $${repair_cost.median} (80% range $${repair_cost.p10}-$${repair_cost.p90}).
Policy: refunds within 30 days of delivery. Prefer repair when it costs less than 60% of the price and the damage doesn't stop the product from working.`,
questions: {
resolution: { type: "choice", instructions: "What should we offer?", criteria: options },
},
})).answers.resolution;
// 3. An LLM writes the reply, from the decision and the facts it needs
const { response } = await env.AI.run("@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3", {
messages: [{
role: "user",
content: `Write a short, warm reply to ${customer_name.value}. Use only these facts: order ${order_id.value}; ` +
`damage: ${damage.value.join(", ")}; what happens next: ${options[choice]}. Under 60 words.`,
}],
});

Each step gets cleaner input than the one before. Clef decides from a five-line summary of typed values instead of a free-form email, which can also be susceptible to prompt injection. The LLM never sees the email, only the decision and the predictions it needs, so there are fewer numbers for it to misuse. Every step is typed and auditable, and only one step generates text. In the all-LLM version of this pipeline, all three steps are generative calls, and every value in the reply has to be checked by hand.

We ran this pipeline against an all-LLM version with GLM-5.3 writing the reply in both. In the all-LLM version, GLM-5.3 also does the extraction and the decision, from the same email, policy and prompts:

Clairic → Clef → GLM-5.3

GLM-5.3 for every step

Latency, end to end

Clairic: 0.46 s

GLM-5.3: 16.1 s

2. Decide

Clef: 0.22 s

3. Reply

GLM-5.3: 18.6 s

GLM-5.3: 16.4 s

Input tokens
